cim: Campus Support and Usability Drive Teacher Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Campus Support and Usability Drive Teacher Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Campus Support and Usability Drive Teacher Adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence

Empirical analysis of educator attitudes in higher education indicates that institutional facilitating conditions and perceived ease of use play central roles in shaping university teachers’ behavioral intentions to adopt generative artificial intelligence tools. In a cross-sectional investigation evaluating survey responses from 315 educators across five application-oriented universities in Anhui, China, researchers identified a substantial direct and indirect network of associations linking institutional support mechanisms to intended instructional technology adoption. Applying an extended structural equation modeling framework based on the classic Technology Acceptance Model, the study demonstrated that while institutional provisions such as infrastructure, training, and governance policies directly encourage adoption intentions, their influence is predominantly transmitted through intermediate cognitive evaluations. Specifically, perceived ease of use emerged as an exceptionally prominent correlational antecedent, carrying greater statistical weight in predicting usage intentions than perceived pedagogical usefulness across the surveyed faculty cohort.

The theoretical framework grounded its inquiry in the structural evolution of technology adoption paradigms, tracing foundational concepts from Davis’s original Technology Acceptance Model through Venkatesh’s Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology. Under conventional acceptance theory, external organizational factors influence user choices indirectly through twin cognitive belief variables, defined as perceived usefulness, reflecting expectations of enhanced job performance, and perceived ease of use, reflecting the degree to which a technology is anticipated to be effortless. While historical implementations in standard educational technologies frequently observed that perceived usefulness dominates user intentions while usability plays a secondary supporting role, generative systems introduce distinct cognitive parameters. The research authors highlighted that tools driven by large language models differ from conventional educational platforms because they rely heavily on natural language prompts, exhibit generative uncertainty, and involve human-machine collaborative content generation, which fundamentally alters how educators perceive instructional utility and operational effort.

To investigate these theoretical relationships, the investigators formulated a multi-tiered structural model comprising four core latent variables: facilitating conditions as the exogenous baseline, perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness as sequential mediators, and behavioral intention as the endogenous outcome. The design incorporated six formal hypothesized paths, testing direct relationships between organizational support and adoption intention, direct links between usability and intention, direct associations between perceived usefulness and intention, and the internal predictive path from ease of use to usefulness. Crucially, the model evaluated two indirect mechanisms: an independent mediation pathway whereby institutional provisions foster adoption exclusively by enhancing operational ease, and a hypothesized serial chain mediation pathway structured as facilitating conditions leading to perceived ease of use, subsequent perceived usefulness, and ultimately behavioral intention.

The study instrument relied on a structured five-point Likert scale adapted from validated acceptance literature and refined to capture generative artificial intelligence dimensions. Seventeen final scale items measured the operational environment across four discrete domains: five items quantified institutional facilitating conditions across technical support, physical hardware, training resources, and institutional policy; four items examined perceived ease of use regarding interface navigation, functional mastery, and troubleshooting prompt dependency; four items evaluated perceived usefulness across instructional preparation, classroom interaction, research assistance, and differentiated instruction; and four items tracked progressive levels of behavioral intention, spanning initial classroom trials to advanced skill acquisition and institutional tool co-development. Before deployment, a panel of five higher education technology specialists reviewed the adapted items for contextual relevance, and a pilot study involving twenty university educators confirmed item clarity, completion duration, and baseline internal consistency.

Data collection utilized an online survey platform that gathered responses from 380 prospective participants, applying automated completion-time monitoring and mandatory response validation. Questionnaires completed in less than 120 seconds or exhibiting uniform response patterns were discarded, leaving a final analytic sample of 315 valid educator responses, representing an effective recovery rate of 82.89 percent. Demographic profiling revealed that the sample was notably concentrated among early-career educators: 58.41 percent identified as female and 41.59 percent as male; 46.35 percent were aged 30 years or younger, 42.22 percent were between 31 and 40 years old, and only 11.43 percent were 41 years or older. Furthermore, 74.60 percent possessed five years or fewer of teaching experience, while 58.41 percent held junior academic titles or below. Disciplinary distribution showed engineering faculty representing 39.37 percent of participants, followed by management at 21.27 percent, arts at 13.65 percent, science at 13.33 percent, and other academic fields at 12.38 percent.

Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling conducted via specialized statistical software demonstrated exceptional internal consistency, reliability, and structural validity across the measurement model. Cronbach’s alpha coefficients across all four constructs exceeded 0.90, ranging from 0.914 for perceived usefulness to 0.940 for facilitating conditions, while Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin sampling adequacy measures surpassed 0.80 alongside statistically significant Bartlett tests of sphericity. Standardized factor loadings across all seventeen measurement items were strong and statistically significant at p < 0.001, spanning from 0.752 to 0.929, with critical ratios well above standard thresholds. Construct reliability was corroborated by composite reliability values between 0.915 and 0.941, matched by McDonald’s omega values, while average variance extracted measures comfortably surpassed the 0.50 benchmark, varying from 0.729 to 0.776. Discriminant validity was supported under the Fornell-Larcker criterion, as the square root of the average variance extracted for each construct exceeded every corresponding inter-construct correlation, as well as under heterotrait-monotrait ratio benchmarks.

Direct structural path estimation confirmed that organizational support structures and usability judgments directly correlate with positive educator intentions. Facilitating conditions demonstrated a significant positive association with teachers’ behavioral intention, yielding a standardized direct coefficient of 0.351 (p < 0.001), while displaying an even stronger association with perceived ease of use (β = 0.713, p < 0.001). Perceived ease of use proved to be a powerful direct predictor of both behavioral intention (β = 0.374, p = 0.001) and perceived usefulness (β = 0.833, p < 0.001). In contrast, perceived usefulness exerted a comparatively modest, though statistically significant, direct influence on behavioral intention (β = 0.191, p = 0.047). Goodness-of-fit indices supported the empirical structural model, with a chi-square to degrees of freedom ratio beneath the conventional cutoff of 3, comparative fit index and Tucker-Lewis index values exceeding 0.96, and root mean square error of approximation measured at 0.07
